blocks.4: Many thick books could surely have been written about Dahl and all the good he did for the people of the parish. He left deep marks, both culturally and materially. In the local history of Gulen, Ivar Kleiva has written a good deal about Dahl and his life's work. Several students have used Dahl and his work as the subject of theses. Aud Randal from Mjømna has had her “major subject paper in history, spring 1991” printed, on the popular educator Niels Griis Alstrup Dahl – a fine piece of work. This spring she submitted her master's thesis “Eivindvigens anden skaber” (The second creator of Eivindvig), which is also very interesting reading. She is still researching the subject, and I hope, and expect, that we will get more in writing from her about Dahl and his work. I will therefore refer to what has already been written about Dahl, and what will probably also come, but will nevertheless include here a little about his almost incredible efforts for his parish.
blocks.5: Dahl was born on the farm Fet in Kvinnherad on 14 March 1778. He matriculated with the grade laudabilis at Bergen Cathedral School in 1796 and graduated in theology with the same grade at the University of Copenhagen in October 1800. On 24 February 1804 he was appointed resident curate in “Evindvik parish”, and on 18 December 1807 parish priest here. He was dean of Ytre Sogn from 1823 to 1847 and a member of the Storting for Nordre Bergenhus county in 1814 (at the extraordinary session that autumn) and in 1827, 1828 and 1830. On 14 October 1825 he received the medal for “civic virtue”, and in 1829 he became a member of the “Royal Society of Sciences in Trondhjem”. He died in Eivindvik on 4 August 1852.
blocks.6: He was married to Hylleborg Hertzberg, born in Finnås on 21 September 1766, died in Eivindvik on 25 May 1848. I have seen very little about her. She is said to have been in poor health, but she must have had a great deal to contend with when we consider everything that went on at the parsonage in her time. She surely had her hands full with the large household. She and Dahl had no children.
blocks.8: Dahl's parsonage, called "Herresalen", around 1890. Photo: Sogn og Fjordane County Archives.
blocks.9: When Dahl became priest here, times were bad in our country, with failed harvests and hard conditions. It seems that the parsonage farm must have been in poor condition. Dahl at once began his great work of cultivation. As mentioned before, he himself told how he had the parsonage bog drained, where he found a great number of oak logs lying so that they dammed up the water and turned the bog into a swamp. He had huge ditches dug, and the stream that comes down from the land where the plantation now stands was laid into a large culvert that runs right past the north side of the house where Dahl lived.
blocks.10: Bishop Neumann, who was very impressed by Dahl's efforts, writes in “Remarks on a journey in Sogn and Søndfjord 1823”, printed in “Budstikken” in 1824, nos. 47–53, among other things: “This land was, unless a great deal of effort was applied, entirely lost to agriculture. But Dahl has defied nature. In every direction where it could serve the purpose he has built stone-lined – I hardly dare call them ditches, but canals, up to 2 ½ ells in height and width, which take up the surplus water and lead it out into the sea. His bog is thus free of water and bears the richest crops, up to fifteenfold oats and twentyfold potatoes. The land is enclosed with large, strong stone walls, and along the walls small cowsheds have been built at intervals, into which the cattle are moved in turn, so that the land below may benefit from the juices of the manure. The large, well-arranged cowshed stands on high pillars, between which the compost is made according to very correctly applied rules.”
blocks.11: Neumann also mentions Dahl's work in collecting “whatever may remain of legends from ancient times” and writes that Dahl had “rare historical and antiquarian knowledge”.
blocks.12: Dahl also had soil carted, and carried, onto the hillocks and worked the parsonage farm up into a model farm. We get a good impression of the effort this required from what “Nordre Bergenhus Amt, vol. II” reports from Neumann's journeys in 1821 and 1822, p. 301. It says, among other things: “...the cultivated land belonging to the parsonage, with its splendid meadows and fields, stands in striking contrast to the surrounding masses of rock, in whose steep ravines there are only scattered patches of level ground strewn with boulders. It is truly a masterpiece of a will devoted to agriculture, shrinking from neither toil nor trouble, that one sees before one here; but however surprising the whole looks against the contrasting surroundings, one would hardly guess what extraordinary efforts and expense it takes to transform this stubborn land, now boggy, now rocky. Many large stones must be sunk, channels dug and canals walled, just to get the soil on which the later work of cultivation can begin; but for that reason smiling fields now shine between the dark, useless mountains as a reward for tireless industry and as proof of the truth that men can defy everything in nature when their enterprise is inspired by perseverance.”
blocks.13: In his book “I alvor og spøk” (In earnest and in jest), the former parish priest here, Øystein Hovden, writes about Dahl, and on page 36 he quotes a saying from “the old priest of Toten”:
blocks.15: happy is he who has a good wife –
blocks.16: but tenfold happy is he who has a slope
blocks.18: in which one can plant potatoes.”
blocks.19: Dahl's parsonage with the church at the top right. Drawing from Illustrert Nyhedsblad of 20 May 1886
blocks.20: Hovden writes that he finds this a strange way of judging, and he does not know whether Dahl would have valued such earthly things in this way. He probably mentions the saying to point out the contribution of the “potato priests” to farming and to emphasise Dahl's great work and interest in cultivation and agriculture. “That he valued the land and the farm very highly”, “we have clear enough proof and testimony of in the unusually great interest he showed precisely in these matters”.
blocks.21: All around the infield, also in Fonnevika, Dahl had a solid grey-stone wall built, about 180–190 cm high and 60–70 cm wide. Ole J. Midtun says, from his grandfather, that it was people from Midtun who did much of the work on this wall. They got 1 krone a day. That was certainly not bad pay at the time. Aud Randal says it is not unlikely that men from Midtun did much of the walling; the Midtun farmers are often mentioned by Dahl. In the local history Kleiva gives the length of the stone wall as 1.5 km, but including Fonnevika it is about 2 km.
blocks.22: Here I must add that Associate Professor Per Linge, when he was here in the summer of 2007, believed that this wall was built by the Huns as early as a few hundred years after Christ, and that the wall was part of a Turkic system of measurement (compare the articles on the name, the stone crosses and Eivindvik as an assembly site). Dahl's work on this wall was to restore it.
blocks.23: In addition to ordinary farming, Dahl experimented with crops that were not common here, for example “lucerne”. A census taken in 1848 states that 36 people then lived at the parsonage and that the livestock was: 4 horses, 39 cows, 167 sheep and 68 goats. On top of that came the crofts, with 1 horse, 51 cows, 78 sheep and 37 goats.
blocks.24: The seed sown at the parsonage was 20 ¾ barrels of oats and 15 ½ barrels of potatoes. By this time Dahl's health was probably somewhat weakened, so the farming was perhaps not quite up to the level it had been in his prime.
blocks.26: In the Storting Dahl was a wise, thorough and fearless debater. At the “first extraordinary Storting”, held in October 1814, he was a clear opponent of the union with Sweden, and he was among the 5 representatives who voted against the union. He could perhaps be a little sharp at times if needed. Neumann's diary from that time says on p. 84 that there were “personal remarks” between Wedel and Dahl and that the president “put them both in their place”.
blocks.27: Øverland's Norwegian history, volume XII, says on p. 429: “A more markedly national position than most other speakers was taken by the priest Nils Dahl from Nordre Bergenhus county, who most firmly advised against the union with the following words:”, and then the speech Dahl gave in the Storting on 20 October 1814 is reproduced. The speech began like this: “As the moment approaches when a subject is to be discussed that will so entirely decide the fortune or misfortune, honour or dishonour of our fatherland's present and future generations; when we, honoured countrymen, are now undoubtedly those on whom the blessings or curses of born and unborn generations will rest, I feel as great a need in my heart as a sacred duty towards myself and towards those of my fellow citizens who authorised me to attend here, to express openly my conviction regarding the most important matter of this moment, namely: the union with Sweden and the election, proposed by the Swedish commissioners, of His Majesty the King of Sweden as King of Norway.”
blocks.28: Further on in the speech it says: “An oath, like every other faith and promise, has not yet become a frivolous children's game among Norway's perhaps less enlightened, but perhaps more honest, dwellers of the rocks and valleys. We all know that the swearing of oaths of our day, now to one king, now to another, is foreign to our honest countrymen, who for centuries have been unbreakably loyal to their ancient royal line, and on whose consciences no perjury, no faithlessness or treason rests. What will be the consequence when a new oath of allegiance is again so suddenly demanded of this people, quite contrary to their wishes and convictions, or even the commands of their conscience?”
blocks.29: The meeting on this 20 October 1814 was held behind closed doors. As we know, there was union with Sweden, despite Dahl's speech.
blocks.31: Dahl built this house in Fonnevika as an example to people of how they ought to build their houses. The house was intended as a parsonage, but instead became the home of the parish clerk and his family. The first permanent school in the parish was also held here. Photo: Audun Skauge.
blocks.32: “Herresalen”, what we call “the old town hall”, was Dahl's home, probably built in 1819. Dahl built the house on Skauge's property in Fonnevika as an example to the farmers of how to put up serviceable houses. It was built in 1814 and was actually intended as a home for Dahl and his family, but they apparently never lived there. Instead the house became the home of the parish clerk and cantor, Anders Furnæs, who was a good helper to Dahl, and from 1820 the first permanent school in the parish was held in this house. In 1835 the first school building in the parish was built at Undertun and the school moved there. Ottar Starheim at NRK Sogn og Fjordane says this was the first school building in our county. At any rate it was the first school building here in Ytre Sogn. Dahl paid for the building with his own money. He also arranged permanent schools in “Brekke sub-parish”, on Byrknesøy in the main parish and in “Husøy sub-parish”. Dahl did a great deal for popular education; he paid for teachers to attend training college and ran his own training of teachers here. Aud Randal writes that Dahl bore all the costs of teacher training himself. These were costs that the school fund bore elsewhere. She also says that on several occasions he bought equipment for the schools. He also worked to get the teachers decent pay. Dahl made a huge contribution to building up the school system in the parish.
blocks.34: It was not only in schooling that Dahl was far ahead and did tremendous work. He also took care of poor relief in the parish in a very good and thorough way; among other things he kept precise plans of where the paupers boarded out on the farms were placed, so that it was always known where they were to stay, and he was careful with records and accounts. His system was considered among the best of its time.
blocks.35: He also organised health care and was something of a doctor himself. Ivar Kleiva writes in the local history that “in time people came to him from all over Ytre Sogn.” Dahl was deeply engaged in the fight against leprosy. He organised and carried out vaccination of the people of the parish against smallpox, and Kleiva writes that during a smallpox epidemic in 1833 the parish here lay “like a protected island”, and “Eivindvik was probably the first parish in Norway to be fully vaccinated”. In an article in the journal of the historical society for Sogn, no. 17, 1955, Kleiva quotes, among other things, from a report Dahl sent to the county: “In Evenvig parish only 2 or 3 individuals were attacked, in every case because they were unwilling to be revaccinated; one was not vaccinated at all, because he claimed to have had natural smallpox as a child, and the result was that he and none other of these 3 fell victim to death.”.
blocks.36: The vaccination was “entirely free”; both Dahl and his helpers, “the parish's cantors and schoolmasters”, felt reward enough in “the joyful experience and awareness that the result of this measure was so beneficial”.
blocks.37: In 1827 Dahl had the first midwife in Ytre Sogn trained and appointed; her name was Ingeborg Svaboe and she lived in Sygnefest.
blocks.39: Dahl fought hard against the evil of drink in the parish. He had several people fined for illegal sale of liquor, among other places here at the church, and he bought up taverns to curb the scourge that drink was for many. He surely found it very painful to watch those he had helped with land consolidation and with buying the land they farmed drink themselves out of house and home. The great work Dahl did with consolidating the farms around the parish is, Kleiva says, “probably unique in the history of Norwegian priests”. Dahl gave two farmers at Midtun, Nicolai Jonson and Jørgen Lasseson, much of the credit for this work, but most of it was surely his own.
blocks.40: This work of Dahl's was noticed too. He had long experience of land consolidation, all the way from 1814, and was among the very foremost. He worked zealously to put an end to all intermixed strips of land. There was much in the land consolidation act of 1821 that he disagreed with and worked to have changed. Many of his views were taken into account in the new act that came in 1857. Where the owners had small incomes, he sometimes paid the costs of moving himself when it was necessary to achieve a good consolidation.
blocks.42: Dahl also spent much time and money on building of various kinds. In addition to the houses he built, he also had roads built, among them a road from Austgulen over Takledalen towards Brekke. He built “Prestekaia” (the parsonage quay) and stone steps from there up to the church so that people could get there more easily. Much of this, and of the upkeep of all the buildings on the parsonage farm, he paid for himself. He had a good income, but spent all of it, and more besides, for the good of the people of his parish. That people complained about him, and perhaps sometimes thought he could be a “hard ruler”, was probably the result of his perhaps occasionally having to use somewhat harsher measures to get his good works done.
blocks.43: Dahl surely had great power and respect among the people. Alongside the large and demanding office of priest and dean (think of the long and exhausting official journeys), he also became the first mayor here when the local government act came in 1837. He held the office of mayor until he asked to be relieved in 1848 because of poor health. He also held the post that today corresponds to the county mayor of Sogn og Fjordane. In 1830 Bishop Neumann wrote that there was a parish library in “Evenvik parish”. Kleiva writes that it started in 1829 and that Dahl gave 134 of his own books to the library.
blocks.44: Everything Dahl took part in and got done must mean that he worked unusually long and exhausting days and had unusual energy and diligence. When we think of the large district, and the long and arduous official journeys he had as priest and dean, one would think that his office must have taken more than his working day; indeed it is incredible what he managed. What he did for his people and his district shows that he was among the very foremost of his time. He won great respect both locally and far beyond, but I do believe that if he had lived in a more central place, he would have been noticed even more and become widely known as the great leader and benefactor he really was. He would then probably have had his memorial long ago. I hope that what has already been written about Dahl, and what will surely be published about him, will become known among the people, and it would be both pleasing and just if this fearless champion of human values and human well-being, both spiritual and material, got his memorial in the garden in front of the house where he lived and organised it all.
blocks.45: Henrik Wergeland came here and visited Dahl in 1832. He was greatly inspired by everything Dahl had achieved and wrote the poem “Evindvig” as a great tribute to Dahl. This poem became well known around the country; it was used, among other things, as set reading for the upper secondary school examinations.
blocks.46: The dean of Ytre Sogn at the time Dahl died, Thomas Erichsen, also wrote a memorial poem to him after Dahl was gone. Since Henrik Wergeland's poem is surely known to everyone, and will be reproduced in the section “Other visitors”, I think I will end my short account of Dahl here with Erichsen's memorial poem:
blocks.47: So sinks into the grave the last
blocks.48: He planted grove on grove with gladness
blocks.50: and raised the fence both deft and firm,
blocks.51: Our whole estate there is a coffin,
blocks.52: And the stony waste became a manor
blocks.53: A little earth and nothing more,
blocks.54: And life and joy what once was dead.
blocks.55: Your goods and gold have passed away,
blocks.56: And the whole region, field on field,
blocks.57: Only dust is left to you.
blocks.58: shall owe Him a farewell song.
blocks.59: And yet we often longed so sorely –
blocks.60: The barren mountain, the naked stones,
blocks.61: While here we suffered and we strove
blocks.62: And the rock cleared and the islet grey
blocks.63: and shed full many a salty tear –
blocks.64: Now stand with fruit on branches green
blocks.65: For the churchyard's rest and peace.
blocks.66: With meadow and field on top.
blocks.67: So He, who here fell asleep, embraced
blocks.68: There little birds in spring shall sing
blocks.69: His grave as surely as a friend.
blocks.70: His funeral song, sweetly, year by year.
blocks.71: Watchful in his calling, the noble one
blocks.72: Yet often He sat with a heavy heart
blocks.73: Has worked as only very few,
blocks.74: For the world rewards good deeds but ill –
blocks.75: His work is done – his name shall live
blocks.76: And silently hid the bitter pain
blocks.77: And reach the village's distant generations.
blocks.78: While He fought for what is true and right.
blocks.79: For bold and brave He bore the staff
blocks.80: Well for Him that the strife is over;
blocks.81: That now stands idle by his grave.
blocks.82: For thorny often was his path.
blocks.83: In the temple's vault, warm and forceful,
blocks.84: With humble mind, with folded hands
blocks.85: His words came from the depths of the heart,
blocks.86: Of Christ's cross he sang at the last.
blocks.87: In the schoolroom, wise and skilled,
blocks.88: Almighty God! in all You send
blocks.90: Make the hour of parting good indeed,
blocks.91: And at every hour and in every place
blocks.92: Then soon forget what here we suffered
blocks.93: He kept his eyes about him.
